table.text: This study was approved by the Princeton Institutional Review Board #15251.
Participants were assigned to one of four conditions: Scientific framing, Religious framing, combined Religious and Scientific framing, or a Control framing for MBCT.

After reading these framings, participants completed a treatment acceptability scale, provided open-ended reflections on why they would or would not be interested in MBCT, and questionnaire measures of existential quest, scriptural literalism, religiosity, and demographics.
Participants aged 18-35 years were recruited through Prolific in July and August 2023.
All participants were based in the USA.

We included a CAPTCHA and multiple-choice attention check question to screen for bots and inattentive participants. 328 participants completed the study and were approved for compensation; after excluding those who failed the attention check, our final usable sample consisted of 305 participants.
After providing informed consent, participants were given the following instruction: "Please imagine you are a patient dealing with an overwhelming amount of stress.
In all conditions, participants were presented with the same introductory description of MBCT.
Participants assigned to the Control condition did not read any additional text beyond the introductory MBCT description.
Following these explanations, participants completed the Treatment Acceptability and Adherence Scale (Milosevic et al., 2015) as our primary measure of treatment acceptability.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We pre-registered (https://osf.io/zsmx4) a target sample size of 300 participants (75 per condition) based on a power analysis indicating that this sample would provide 80% power to detect small-to-moderate (f = 0.17) interaction effects in a 2 × 2 ANOVA. This sample size is also consistent with prior work examining how religious framing influences willingness to engage in mindfulness-based interventions (Palitsky et al., 2022). Participants aged 18-35 years were recruited through Prolific in July and August 2023. All participants were based in the USA.

We pre-registered a target sample size of 705 participants (https://osf.io/xawkn). We aimed to match the sample size of Study 1, and given the availability of additional resources, we further increased the sample to maximize power to detect small effects in a one-way ANOVA (f = 0.12). Participants aged 18-35 were recruited using Prolific in March 2024. All participants were based in the US. Participants must have passed an initial CAPTCHA to access the study, and two attention checks were included during the study. First, after viewing the introduction to MBCT, participants completed a multiple-choice question asking which psychological therapy had been described. Second, participants reported how many portions of meat they typically ate per week and, later in the survey, were asked to indicate which food category they had previously been asked about. 767 participants completed the study; after excluding 62 participants who failed one or more attention checks, the final analyzed sample consisted of N = 705. As in Study 1, this study was conducted prior to the widespread adoption of AI tools, so results are unlikely to have been influenced by them. Participant demographic information is reported in Table 1.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Accepting Mindfulness-Based Interventions: Do Religious vs Scientific Framings Affect Patients’ Perceptions?
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
Despite their benefits and secular approach, there have been concerns about whether the origins of mindfulness and an individual's religious background might interfere with their acceptance of mindfulness interventions (Palitsky & Kaplan 2021). This project aims to answer whether religious-based framing compared to scientific-based framing of mindfulness based interventions affect a patient's acceptance and anticipated adherence to these interventions. This study will also examine whether an individual’s religiosity intensity affects the acceptability and anticipated adherence ratings toward mindfulness based interventions.

Research has suggested that people prescribe different values to scientific and religious explanations of everyday phenomena (e.g., explanations for existential questions such as why people suffer, and what the meaning of life is?) and that these values are moderated by their own levels of religiosity. A recent study that recruited participants who were primarily Christian (54%) or of another spiritual identity (26%) found that, on average, participants gave scientific explanations more epistemic merit (i.e., based on fact and logic), and they give religious explanations more non-epistemic merits (i.e., based on social, moral, and emotional ideals) (Davoodi & Lombrozo, 2022). Although this overall effect was observed, participants’ religious identities moderated how much non-epistemic and epistemic merit they gave a religious explanation. Less religious participants gave higher epistemic ratings to scientific explanations than individuals with high religiosity ratings. In contrast, more religious participants gave higher non-epistemic ratings to religious explanations than low religious individuals. The experiment highlighted how individuals give both religious and scientific explanations different values when it comes to explaining their surroundings and everyday life.

Religious views have also been shown to affect the ways in which people interpret psychological treatments. Specifically, Walker et al., (2011) found that Christian patients seeking psychotherapy at religiously oriented psychotherapy centers tended to bring their religious commitments to therapy. The religious participants in the study described being very likely to bring up their religious and spiritual concerns to psychotherapy despite acknowledging that these concerns were not the root of the psychological problem for which they sought help (Walker et al., 2011). Although the population studied was exclusively Christian, and particularly those seeking help from a religiously based therapist, findings still suggest that, overall, Christian-identifying individuals may want to have their religious beliefs acknowledged during psychotherapy. 

Furthermore, religion has been shown to play a role in treatment adherence. A meta-analysis that examined religious beliefs and adherence to treatments found that there were beneficial effects of patient religiosity on treatment adherence for individuals experiencing addiction and depression (Zagożdżon & Magdalena, 2017). It is important to note, though, that the study found a negative effect of religiosity on treatment adherence for those diagnosed with schizophrenia. In addition, there is some evidence that more religious individuals show greater adherence to religious-based therapies over non-religious therapies (Koenig et al., 2015). Since 69% of the US population identifies with a religion (Pew Research Center, 2021), it is essential to understand the effects that an individual’s religious identity might have on their adoption of psychotherapy.

Mindfulness-based psychological interventions (MBIs) have been demonstrated to be effective in helping people deal with an array of psychological concerns (Teasdale et al.,  2000, Kabat-Zinn et al., 1985). These MBIs borrow heavily from South and Southeast Asian traditions and religions. These established forms of MBIs are secular but also do not cater to the spiritual views of other religious groups, especially those popular in the United States (i.e., Christianity). Misconceptions concerning MBIs and their presumed religious ties could prevent individuals who identify with non-Eastern religions from obtaining the physical and psychological benefits that MBIs can provide. 

The current study will manipulate the type of explanation participants receive regarding the origin of one specific mindfulness-based intervention (mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, MBCT). We will randomly assign participants to one of four conditions that manipulate the presentation of mindfulness-based interventions in a 2 x 2 design. This results in four conditions as follows: Scientific Only, Religious Only, Scientific and Religious, and None/Control. We will then test how these conditions affect participants’ acceptance of and anticipated adherence to MBCT if they were experiencing overwhelming distress and were recommended MBCT by their primary healthcare provider. We will also test whether constructs central to religious identity (i.e., the centrality of religiosity (CRS), existential quest (EQ), and pre-occupation with the truth of one’s religion (TTT)) interact with the explanation given to predict acceptance/adherence (TAAS) scores.

Our primary hypotheses, which are based on the assumption that the majority of religious participants in our study will identify as Christian*, are as follows:

- (H1) There will be main effects of both Religious [present vs absent] and Scientific [present vs absent] origin framings. Religious framings will be negatively associated with treatment acceptance scores, while scientific framings will be positively associated with treatment acceptance scores. There are reasons to hypothesize several possible outcomes for the interaction effect. We could observe an interaction such that the scientific condition combined with the religious explanation in fact make the treatment more acceptable. Conversely, combining them could weaken the positive benefit of the scientific framing.  Finally, we could also expect no interaction, suggesting that the effect of each framing merely adds to the other. As such, we do not have strong hypotheses regarding the interaction.

-  (H2) There will be an interaction effect between the Centrality of religiosity scores and the framing, whereby individuals with high Centrality of religiosity scores will give religious framings lower treatment acceptance scores than individuals with low Centrality of religiosity scores.

* We expect this to be the case since Christianity is the largest religion in the United States (Pew Research Center, 2021). If the majority of participants are non-Christian identifying we will still run the same analysis but will have different hypotheses. For example, if the majority of participants are Buddhist then we would expect there to be a positive association between treatment acceptance scores and religious framing and a positive interaction effect between centrality of religiosity scores and treatment acceptance scores.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Participants' acceptance and anticipated adherence to MBCT will be the primary dependent variable. This will be measured using the Treatment Acceptability and Adherence Scale (TAAS; Milosevic et al., 2015), which will be completed after participants read the MBCT explanation. The scale was designed to measure perceptions of psychotherapeutic interventions for anxiety disorders and related problems. We have modified the wording of items 6, 8, and 9 to refer to ‘mental health difficulties’ rather than ‘fear/anxiety’.

The Centrality of Religiosity Scale (CRS): This is a 15-item scale that measures 5 different aspects of the participant’s religious habits and identity which include an individual’s “public practice, private practice, religious experience, ideology, and their intellectual dimensions” (Huber et al., 2012).

Existential Quest (EQ): This is a 9-item scale that is used to measure an individual’s openness to answers concerning existential questions which might not align with their beliefs. It assesses how open individuals are to religious/spiritual beliefs that are not their own (Van Pachterbeke et al., 2012). Note that this scale is collected for supplemental analyses.

The Truth of Texts and Teachings (TTT): This is a 5-item subscale of the Religious Schema Scale used to measure the scriptural literalism of an individual. It highlights how attached individuals are to their religious teachings and scriptures (Streib et al., 2010). Note that this scale is collected for supplemental analyses.

Religious/Spiritual Identity: We will ask participants to disclose their religious/spiritual identity by selecting a religion from pre-determined lists. If their identity is not represented, they can type it in manually using the ‘Other’ option.
table.study_design_overview:
We will randomly assign participants to one of four conditions that manipulate the presentation of mindfulness-based interventions in a 2 x 2 design. This results in four conditions that are as follows: Scientific only, Religious only, Scientific and Religious, and None/Control. The order of the text in the combined “Scientific and Religious” condition will be randomized such that half of the participants in that condition receive the scientific framing before the religious framing and vice versa for the other half.

Before reading these framings, all participants will read a paragraph explaining the components of MBCT (Kuyken et al., 2010) in neutral language (i.e., not indicating a religious or scientific background). The “None/Control” condition will only include this paragraph and no other information.
table.statistical_tests:
Analyses will be conducted using R. 

H1) How does the religious and/or scientific framing of MBCT affect treatment acceptability? 

A two-way ANOVA will be used. It will consist of a 2 [scientific explanation: absent vs present] x 2 [religious explanation: absent vs present] ANOVA, with treatment acceptance scores as the dependent variable.  Post-hoc t-tests will be used to explore significant effects.

As noted above, we hypothesize both the main effects of religious and scientific framings, but we do not have strong hypotheses regarding an interaction. 

H2) Do religiosity scores moderate the impact of religious and/or scientific framings on treatment acceptance?

We will conduct a 2 [scientific explanation: absent vs present] x 2 [religious explanation: absent vs present] ANOVA with the centrality of religiosity scores as a covariate and treatment acceptance scores as the dependent variable. We will unpack significant interactions through follow-up analyses.

As noted above, we hypothesize there will be a negative interaction between CRS scores and treatment acceptance scores, meaning those who score higher on the CRS survey will rate the religious-framed questions more negatively.

Exploratory analyses:
We will collect further data surrounding religiosity. We are not pre-registering primary analyses with this data, though we will conduct exploratory analyses to investigate the following questions:

Do TTT scores moderate the association between framing and TAAS scores? 

Do EQ scores moderate the association between framing and TAAS scores? 

Additionally, if there is a sufficiently large sample of multiple religious groups, we will explore whether religious/spiritual identity moderates the effect of framing on TAAS scores.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
The study is short. We will use a CAPTCHA test at the start of the survey to rule out potential bots, and an attention task following the randomized explanation will be used to see whether participants paid attention to the explanation. This attention task will ask a simple question concerning the topic of their intervention explanation: “Which psychological therapy was just described?”. Participants who do not correctly answer the CAPTCHA or this attention check will be excluded. 

Before conducting analyses, we will test the assumptions of our statistical tests and make appropriate adjustments [i.e., transformations, use of non-parametric tests] to ensure the assumptions of tests are met.
table.sample_size:
We will recruit participants until we obtain a usable sample size of 300 participants (75 per condition). Prolific will be used to recruit participants aged 18-35 years who are based in the US. 

A power analysis using Superpower in R indicated that a sample size of 300 (75 per condition) will give 80% power for detecting ordinal and disordinal interactions in a 2x2 ANOVA of size f = 0.16.

table.name: Accepting Mindfulness-Based Interventions: Do Religious vs Scientific Framings Affect Patients’ Perceptions?

table.title: Does addressing concerns about mindfulness-based interventions improve acceptability?
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
Does addressing patients’ concerns about MBCT lead to greater acceptance of MBCT?

- We hypothesize that addressing concerns about MBCT will lead to higher treatment acceptance, as measured by TAAS ratings. Specifically, we hypothesize that Condition 1 (targeted concern responses) & Condition 2 (all concern responses) will have higher TAAS ratings than the control Condition 3 (no concern responses).

- We do not have a strong hypothesis as to whether Condition 1 or 2 will have a greater effect on acceptance ratings. Condition 1 could be more effective as it only addresses the concerns reported by the participants. Although Condition 2 does this as well, there is a possibility that addressing non-specified concerns could lead to participants thinking more about these potential stresses. However, it could also be the case that providing responses to all possible concerns increases a participant's acceptance of the intervention.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Acceptance and anticipated adherence to MBCT: Our primary dependent variable will be measured using the Treatment Acceptability and Adherence Scale (TAAS; Milosevic et al., 2015). The scale was designed to measure perceptions of psychotherapeutic interventions for anxiety disorders and related problems. We have modified the wording of items 6, 8, and 9 to refer to ‘mental health difficulties’ rather than ‘fear/anxiety’. Total scores from this measure will be used as our primary DV for this study.

The Centrality of Religiosity Scale (CRS): This is a 15-item scale that measures 5 different aspects of the participant’s religious habits and identity which include an individual’s “public practice, private practice, religious experience, ideology, and their intellectual dimensions” (Huber et al., 2012).
table.study_design_overview:
Condition #1 will address only the concerns participants selected as concerns. 
Condition #2 will address all 9 concerns, regardless of how many and which concerns participants select.
Condition #3 will be our control condition and will not address any concerns.
table.statistical_tests:
H1: Does addressing participants’ concerns about MBCT lead to greater acceptance of MBCT?
We will use a one-way ANOVA to test whether there are differences in TAAS scores between the three conditions. If significant, we will run post-hoc t-tests to explore group differences.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
We will use a CAPTCHA test at the start of the survey to rule out potential bots, and two additional attention checks are included in the survey. Participants who do not correctly answer the CAPTCHA or either of the attention checks will be excluded from analyses.

Before conducting analyses, we will test the assumptions of our statistical tests and make appropriate adjustments [i.e., transformations, use of non-parametric tests] to ensure the assumptions of tests are met.
table.sample_size:
We will recruit participants until we obtain a usable sample size of 705 participants (235 per condition). Prolific will be used to recruit participants aged 18-35 years who are based in the US. 

We wanted to ensure we were powered for at least small-to-medium effects (f = .15) but had sufficient funding to run up to 705 Ps (235 Ps/condition). Thus we set our a priori target usable sample size as 705, which provides 80% power to detect effects as small as f = .12
table.additional_comments:
We may also conduct the following exploratory analyses to test whether religiosity relates to MBCT outcomes:

- We will add religiosity as a factor to the ANOVA testing associations between Condition and TAAS scores, and follow up with post-hoc tests if indicated.

- Test for correlations between religiosity and the strength of each of the 9 concerns during the initial concern ratings.

This project aims to answer whether religious-based framing compared to scientific-based framing of mindfulness based interventions affect a patient's acceptance and anticipated adherence to these interventions. This study will also examine whether an individual’s religiosity intensity affects the acceptability and anticipated adherence ratings toward mindfulness based interventions.

Research has suggested that people prescribe different values to scientific and religious explanations of everyday phenomena (e.g., explanations for existential questions such as why people suffer, and what the meaning of life is?) and that these values are moderated by their own levels of religiosity. A recent study that recruited participants who were primarily Christian (54%) or of another spiritual identity (26%) found that, on average, participants gave scientific explanations more epistemic merit (i.e., based on fact and logic), and they give religious explanations more non-epistemic merits (i.e., based on social, moral, and emotional ideals) (Davoodi & Lombrozo, 2022). Although this overall effect was observed, participants’ religious identities moderated how much non-epistemic and epistemic merit they gave a religious explanation. Less religious participants gave higher epistemic ratings to scientific explanations than individuals with high religiosity ratings. In contrast, more religious participants gave higher non-epistemic ratings to religious explanations than low religious individuals. The experiment highlighted how individuals give both religious and scientific explanations different values when it comes to explaining their surroundings and everyday life.

Religious views have also been shown to affect the ways in which people interpret psychological treatments. Specifically, Walker et al., (2011) found that Christian patients seeking psychotherapy at religiously oriented psychotherapy centers tended to bring their religious commitments to therapy. The religious participants in the study described being very likely to bring up their religious and spiritual concerns to psychotherapy despite acknowledging that these concerns were not the root of the psychological problem for which they sought help (Walker et al., 2011). Although the population studied was exclusively Christian, and particularly those seeking help from a religiously based therapist, findings still suggest that, overall, Christian-identifying individuals may want to have their religious beliefs acknowledged during psychotherapy.

Furthermore, religion has been shown to play a role in treatment adherence. A meta-analysis that examined religious beliefs and adherence to treatments found that there were beneficial effects of patient religiosity on treatment adherence for individuals experiencing addiction and depression (Zagożdżon & Magdalena, 2017). It is important to note, though, that the study found a negative effect of religiosity on treatment adherence for those diagnosed with schizophrenia. In addition, there is some evidence that more religious individuals show greater adherence to religious-based therapies over non-religious therapies (Koenig et al., 2015). Since 69% of the US population identifies with a religion (Pew Research Center, 2021), it is essential to understand the effects that an individual’s religious identity might have on their adoption of psychotherapy.

Mindfulness-based psychological interventions (MBIs) have been demonstrated to be effective in helping people deal with an array of psychological concerns (Teasdale et al., 2000, Kabat-Zinn et al., 1985). These MBIs borrow heavily from South and Southeast Asian traditions and religions. These established forms of MBIs are secular but also do not cater to the spiritual views of other religious groups, especially those popular in the United States (i.e., Christianity). Misconceptions concerning MBIs and their presumed religious ties could prevent individuals who identify with non-Eastern religions from obtaining the physical and psychological benefits that MBIs can provide.

The current study will manipulate the type of explanation participants receive regarding the origin of one specific mindfulness-based intervention (mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, MBCT). We will randomly assign participants to one of four conditions that manipulate the presentation of mindfulness-based interventions in a 2 x 2 design. This results in four conditions as follows: Scientific Only, Religious Only, Scientific and Religious, and None/Control. We will then test how these conditions affect participants’ acceptance of and anticipated adherence to MBCT if they were experiencing overwhelming distress and were recommended MBCT by their primary healthcare provider. We will also test whether constructs central to religious identity (i.e., the centrality of religiosity (CRS), existential quest (EQ), and pre-occupation with the truth of one’s religion (TTT)) interact with the explanation given to predict acceptance/adherence (TAAS) scores.

Our primary hypotheses, which are based on the assumption that the majority of religious participants in our study will identify as Christian*, are as follows:

- (H1) There will be main effects of both Religious [present vs absent] and Scientific [present vs absent] origin framings. Religious framings will be negatively associated with treatment acceptance scores, while scientific framings will be positively associated with treatment acceptance scores. There are reasons to hypothesize several possible outcomes for the interaction effect. We could observe an interaction such that the scientific condition combined with the religious explanation in fact make the treatment more acceptable. Conversely, combining them could weaken the positive benefit of the scientific framing. Finally, we could also expect no interaction, suggesting that the effect of each framing merely adds to the other. As such, we do not have strong hypotheses regarding the interaction.

- (H2) There will be an interaction effect between the Centrality of religiosity scores and the framing, whereby individuals with high Centrality of religiosity scores will give religious framings lower treatment acceptance scores than individuals with low Centrality of religiosity scores.

* We expect this to be the case since Christianity is the largest religion in the United States (Pew Research Center, 2021). If the majority of participants are non-Christian identifying we will still run the same analysis but will have different hypotheses. For example, if the majority of participants are Buddhist then we would expect there to be a positive association between treatment acceptance scores and religious framing and a positive interaction effect between centrality of religiosity scores and treatment acceptance scores.", "Participants' acceptance and anticipated adherence to MBCT will be the primary dependent variable. This will be measured using the Treatment Acceptability and Adherence Scale (TAAS; Milosevic et al., 2015), which will be completed after participants read the MBCT explanation. The scale was designed to measure perceptions of psychotherapeutic interventions for anxiety disorders and related problems. We have modified the wording of items 6, 8, and 9 to refer to ‘mental health difficulties’ rather than ‘fear/anxiety’.

The Centrality of Religiosity Scale (CRS): This is a 15-item scale that measures 5 different aspects of the participant’s religious habits and identity which include an individual’s “public practice, private practice, religious experience, ideology, and their intellectual dimensions” (Huber et al., 2012).

Existential Quest (EQ): This is a 9-item scale that is used to measure an individual’s openness to answers concerning existential questions which might not align with their beliefs. It assesses how open individuals are to religious/spiritual beliefs that are not their own (Van Pachterbeke et al., 2012). Note that this scale is collected for supplemental analyses.

The Truth of Texts and Teachings (TTT): This is a 5-item subscale of the Religious Schema Scale used to measure the scriptural literalism of an individual. It highlights how attached individuals are to their religious teachings and scriptures (Streib et al., 2010). Note that this scale is collected for supplemental analyses.

Religious/Spiritual Identity: We will ask participants to disclose their religious/spiritual identity by selecting a religion from pre-determined lists. If their identity is not represented, they can type it in manually using the ‘Other’ option.", "We will randomly assign participants to one of four conditions that manipulate the presentation of mindfulness-based interventions in a 2 x 2 design. A two-way ANOVA will be used. It will consist of a 2 [scientific explanation: absent vs present] x 2 [religious explanation: absent vs present] ANOVA, with treatment acceptance scores as the dependent variable. Post-hoc t-tests will be used to explore significant effects.

We will conduct a 2 [scientific explanation: absent vs present] x 2 [religious explanation: absent vs present] ANOVA with the centrality of religiosity scores as a covariate and treatment acceptance scores as the dependent variable. We will unpack significant interactions through follow-up analyses.

As noted above, we hypothesize there will be a negative interaction between CRS scores and treatment acceptance scores, meaning those who score higher on the CRS survey will rate the religious-framed questions more negatively.

Do TTT scores moderate the association between framing and TAAS scores?

marginal.title: Marginal Significance
marginal.summary_text: You described 4 effects with terms related to 'marginally significant'.

table.text: The Scientific × existential quest interaction effect was marginally significant, F(1, 297) = 3.13, p = .078.
We unpacked this marginally significant interaction by examining the correlation between existential quest and treatment acceptability within each level of Scientific framing.

Thus, religiosity appeared to shape baseline openness to MBCT independent of how it was introduced to participants, although the marginal significance of the overall effect means that it should be interpreted cautiously.

When religiosity (CRS scores; mean-centered) was added to the model, there was a significant main effect of religiosity, F(1,699) = 11.08, p < .001, a marginally significant effect of condition, F(2,699) = 2.96, p = .052, and no interaction, F(2,699) = .326, p = .722.

stat_check.title: StatCheck
stat_check.summary_text: We detected no errors in t-tests or F-tests.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps > .114", "ps > .071", "ps > .162", 
"ps > .260", "ps > .169", "ps > .101"), Text = c("These results held when analyzing the subsample of N = 121 participants who identified as Christian, Fs < 2.53, ps > .114.", 
"No other main or interaction effects were significant, Fs < 3.32, ps > .071.", 
"No other effects were significant, ps > .162.", "In the model testing scriptural literalism as a moderator, no effects were significant, ps > .260.", 
"As above, the main effects of Scientific and Religious framing, and their interaction, were not significant, ps > .169.", 
"No other correlations reached significance, ps > .101 (Supplementary Material Table S3)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 171 columns across 3 data files.
#### Issues Identified

1 file/column combination has at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = "concerns_study1.csv", Column = "text_TAAS", Issues = "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 127 characters, 100% distinct) may contain...
↔️ Whitespace — 25 values with leading/trailing whitespace: \"I used mindfulness in ..."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding

186 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **90 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 2 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

findings.detail: 25 values with leading/trailing whitespace: "I used mindfulness in the past when dealing with panic disorder in college. This treatment helped me tremendously and I no longer have panic attacks. However not every person will react the same way to this therapy and may find medication beneficial as well, as I now use anti depressants to manage my depression and suicidal thoughts. Mindfulness requires dedication and compliance ", "As an agnostic, I don't have a lot of interest in the religious or spiritual aspects of the program (and this would apply if it were Christian or had a more ""Western"" religion, to be clear). However, I think I'd like to at least give it a try, and I think the emphasis on distancing yourself from negative thoughts and mindfulness could be very helpful. ", "As a militant Antitheist, I have no respect for anything deriving from religion. Furthermore, I will report the therapist for promotion of religion, which is disgusting and unethical ", "Weekly group sessions and mindful meditations would be difficult for me. if I am in a time of high stress, the last thing I will be able to do is take myself into a group setting and try to focus. I think that guided meditation would be interesting, but I have never been able to feel that I have successfully meditated before in both guided and unguided sessions. ", "I like how it re-wires your thinking, in order to create new habits and to overall be more mindful. I just also know that when you are depressed, it is hard to get in a mindset where you truly want to take action, because it can be hard to see the point. ", "I think mindfulness can be powerful for helping with stress and anxiety, but I'm not sure I would like any group therapies, especially as the first treatment option. ", "I like the mindfulness portion of this therapy, however I have heard that CBT in general is not super effective for autistic individuals who need a more somatic based approach ", "The therapy seems non-invasive and could be something that many can make progress through if given the right effort and willfullness. Still, it also just sounds like someone saying to ""just breathe"" it out while the patient could be going through a mental/medical crisis that needs greater intervention than meditation. ", "I do think mindfulness is helpful, but there is a limit on how helpful being aware and combating negative thoughts can be when you might be dealing with poverty, debt, oppression, abuse etc. ", "The meditation aspect seems like it would be particularly helpful in reducing stress, while cognitive therapy would augment this calming effect to provide more resiliency in stressful situations in the future. I can't see very many downsides to it; I would only hesitate to recommend it to a friend because I would need to complete it to evaluate whether it really works well or not, but I'd be rather optimistic going in, at least. "

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 2 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  1 of 2 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  10 installable dependencies detected.
- 7 statistics stored from the extracted output; 1 of 36 reported tests matched (2.8%).

summary_table.ethics_statements: This study was approved by the Princeton Institutional Review Board #15251.
live_data_statements: Participants were assigned to one of four conditions: Scientific framing, Religious framing, combined Religious and Scientific framing, or a Control framing for MBCT.

After reading these framings, participants completed a treatment acceptability scale, provided open-ended reflections on why they would or would not be interested in MBCT, and questionnaire measures of existential quest, scriptural literalism, religiosity, and demographics.
Participants aged 18-35 years were recruited through Prolific in July and August 2023.
All participants were based in the USA.

We included a CAPTCHA and multiple-choice attention check question to screen for bots and inattentive participants. 328 participants completed the study and were approved for compensation; after excluding those who failed the attention check, our final usable sample consisted of 305 participants.
After providing informed consent, participants were given the following instruction: "Please imagine you are a patient dealing with an overwhelming amount of stress.
In all conditions, participants were presented with the same introductory description of MBCT.
Participants assigned to the Control condition did not read any additional text beyond the introductory MBCT description.
Following these explanations, participants completed the Treatment Acceptability and Adherence Scale (Milosevic et al., 2015) as our primary measure of treatment acceptability.

Then, participants completed questionnaires assessing religiosity (Centrality of Religiosity; Huber & Huber, 2012), existential quest (Existential Quest scale; Van Pachterbeke et al., 2012), and scriptural literalism (Truth of Text and Teaching; Streib et al., 2010), which were presented in a random order.
Finally, participants completed a demographics questionnaire.
Participants aged 18-35 were recruited using Prolific in March 2024.
All participants were based in the US.
First, after viewing the introduction to MBCT, participants completed a multiple-choice question asking which psychological therapy had been described.

Second, participants reported how many portions of meat they typically ate per week and, later in the survey, were asked to indicate which food category they had previously been asked about. 767 participants completed the study; after excluding 62 participants who failed one or more attention checks, the final analyzed sample consisted of N = 705.
After providing informed consent and passing the CAPTCHA task, participants completed a survey administered via Qualtrics.
After reading this description, participants were shown the nine concerns that emerged from qualitative coding in Study 1 (Table 4).

Participants were instructed to "Select all the concerns that you have with the proposed Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy" using checkboxes and could choose as many or as few concerns as they wished.
Next, participants were randomized into one of three conditions:
Finally, all participants completed the TAAS, followed by an open-text question asking what interested or did not interest them about MBCT.

In Study 1, religiosity showed a marginal positive association with acceptability, and here we found that this relationship was significant, regardless of what condition participants were assigned to.
First, our participants were not clinical samples who were seeking treatment.
Informed consent was obtained from all participants included in the study.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order

No ordering signal (no data dependency, `source()` call, or numeric filename prefix) distinguishes the run order of these files. They may need to run in a specific order that could not be determined automatically — check this before running.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:2, File = c("analysis.R", "analysis.Rmd"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "—"), Basis = c("none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, 
-2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 1 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 

*a script hit a `could not find function "..."` error; we added the `library()` calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("analysis.R", "analysis.Rmd"), Outcome = c("errored", 
"ran_ok"), Detail = c("undefined_variable", ""), "Time (s)" = c(4.1, 
5.9)), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "analysis.R", "Missing variable" = "study1", 
    "Defined in" = "(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`library()` calls added**

**1 script uses functions from packages it does not load itself.** The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. To run it we added the `library()` calls below at the top. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after adding `library()` calls it should make itself**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "analysis.R", "library() calls added" = "library(tidyverse), library(car), library(rstatix), library(effsize), library(readxl), library(emmeans), library(knitr), library(broom)"), row.names = "analysis.R", class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
